routes: The Amorites, among whom Baal Hadad and El are worshipped, invade Mesopotamia (end of the Early Bronze Age)
marks: The Ebla tablets from Tell Mardikh, of the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE, list offerings to El, Baal and Dagon: the earliest evidence of Canaanite religion.
The inscriptions of Idrimi, king of Alalakh in the 15th century BCE, shed light on Canaanite religion.
More than three hundred tablets of about 1275 BCE, found at Ras Shamra since 1928, preserve the Baal Cycle and other myths, prayers and rites.
The Mesha Stele (c. 850 BCE), one of the few sources for religion in the southern Levant beyond Israel and Judah.
A Phoenician bilingual inscription of about 720 BCE, one of the sources for Phoenician religion.
The Carthage Tariff of about 200 BCE records Punic religious practice.
Punic religious practices outlived the Roman conquest, in some places until the 4th century CE.
notes: In the Early Bronze Age the peoples of the southern Levant sacrifice animals, among them donkeys brought from Egypt, at sites such as Tell es-Safi.
The Ebla tablets list offerings to El, Baal and Dagon, the earliest written evidence of the Canaanite gods; Amorite personal names honour the same deities.
In the Middle and Late Bronze Age Egyptian, Hurrian and Mitannian gods leave their mark: Baal is identified with Set and with Teshub, and the Hurrian goddess Hebat is worshipped in Jerusalem.
At Ugarit more than three hundred texts of about 1275 BCE record the myths of El, Baal, Anat and Mot, with hymns, prayers and ritual lists; the city is destroyed around 1200 BCE.
As Egyptian power over Canaan declines in the Iron Age, peoples and cities gather round patron gods: Chemosh of Moab, Milcom of Ammon, Qos of Edom, Yahweh of Israel, Melqart of Tyre, Eshmun of Sidon.
From the 9th century BCE Phoenician settlers carry their religion west, to Carthage, North Africa, southern Spain, Sardinia, western Sicily and Malta.
In the Hellenistic period Greek religion spreads alongside Canaanite traditions, and Canaanite gods are given the names of their Greek equivalents.
Rome conquers the Punic lands in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE, but Punic religious practice continues there.
Punic religious practices survive in some places until the 4th century CE.
